one_liner: Go port of XXH3 64/128-bit hashing with avo-generated SSE2/AVX2/AVX-512/NEON accumulators; no measured win over C xxHash.
what_it_does: A Go implementation of the XXH3 non-cryptographic hash whose output matches upstream xxHash v0.8.0 and later. One-shot functions (Hash, HashString, Hash128, HashString128 and the *Seed variants) return a uint64 or a Uint128, and Hasher and Hasher128 are streaming hash.Hash/hash.Hash64 implementations with seed support. It is a Go library for Go programs that want XXH3 without cgo, not a replacement for the C library inside C or C++ code; custom secrets (XXH3_64bits_withSecret) are not exposed, only seeds.
how_it_is_fast: Inputs up to 240 bytes take XXH3's short paths as straight-line Go with bits.Mul64 128-bit multiply-fold steps and no loops below 129 bytes. Longer inputs run the 8-lane stripe accumulator (acc += lo32(data^secret) * hi32(data^secret), plus a scramble every 1 KiB block) in avo-generated assembly: SSE2, AVX2 or AVX-512 on amd64, chosen at run time with klauspost/cpuid (AVX-512 only from 1 KiB), and NEON on arm64 (added January 2026); every other GOARCH uses a scalar Go accumulator. Hash and HashString reinterpret the slice or string header through unsafe so no copy or allocation happens per call.
when_to_use: Go services that need fast non-cryptographic hashing (content checksums, dedup keys, sharding, cache keys) without cgo: the 2026 README shows 1.2-3.9 ns per hash for 0-128 byte inputs and 96 GB/s (AVX2) or 149 GB/s (AVX-512) at 100 KB on a Ryzen 9 9950X.
When Go code must produce the same XXH3 or XXH128 values as C, C++ or Rust peers: the repo's compat tests check Go output against vectors printed by the upstream C library.
When you need 128-bit XXH3 or seeded XXH3 in Go; cespare/xxhash, the usual Go hash dependency, implements XXH64 only.

amd64 and arm64 deployments, where the SIMD paths exist; go-simd/xxhash's own measurements put zeebo/xxh3 ahead of it on Apple-silicon arm64 (about 22.9 vs 15.2 GB/s at 64 KiB) and slightly ahead on amd64 at 64 KiB.
when_not_to_use: Inside C or C++ programs: call upstream xxHash directly. Nothing in the repository times the C library, so there is no evidence this port beats it (upstream reports 59.4 GB/s AVX2 and 31.5 GB/s SSE2 on an i7-9700K with Clang 10; the port's i7-8850H table shows 44.3 and 25.3 GB/s on different hardware, which is not a comparison).
Targets other than amd64 and arm64 (ppc64le, s390x, riscv64, loong64) get only the scalar Go accumulator; go-simd/xxhash measured 10333 MB/s against this package's 4554 MB/s on an IBM z15 at 64 KiB.
Code that needs XXH3 with a caller-supplied secret, or XXH32/XXH64: only the default secret and seeds are supported.

Seeded hashing of many 241 B to tens-of-KB inputs: each seeded one-shot call re-derives the 192-byte secret (512 B SSE2: 20.3 vs 11.2 ns unseeded); reuse a NewSeed Hasher instead, or wait for open PR #28.
Anything adversarial (hash-flooding resistance, integrity against attackers): XXH3 is not a keyed cryptographic hash.

integration.form: module (Go package github.com/zeebo/xxh3, plain Go assembly files, no cgo)
integration.dependencies: github.com/klauspost/cpuid/v2 (CPU feature detection on amd64); github.com/zeebo/assert for tests only
integration.min_toolchain: Go 1.22 (go.mod); assembly is pre-generated, avo is only needed to regenerate it
integration.platforms: amd64 (SSE2 baseline, AVX2 and AVX-512F selected at run time), arm64 (NEON); all other GOARCH values build with the scalar Go path (the Makefile vets 386, arm, windows and darwin targets)
integration.thread_safety: One-shot functions are pure and safe to call concurrently; Hasher and Hasher128 hold mutable state and, like any hash.Hash, are not documented as safe for concurrent use
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — produces the same XXH3/XXH128 values as C xxHash v0.8.0+, but through a Go API; it does not replace the C library in C or C++ code

gotchas: Run-time dispatch always prefers AVX2 over SSE2 and switches to AVX-512 at 1 KiB, yet the README's own Ryzen 9 9950X columns show SSE2 faster than AVX2 at 241 B (7.95 vs 11.3 ns) and 512 B (11.2 vs 14.1 ns) and AVX-512 slower than SSE2 at 1024 B (23.9 vs 20.7 ns). The per-ISA columns come from benchmarks that force each path (withSSE2/withAVX2 overrides in hash64_test.go), so the default path is not the fastest column between 241 B and 1 KiB on that CPU.

Benchmark harness: the README 'Rate' column above 240 B is the forced scalar Go accumulator (withGeneric in BenchmarkFixed64), not what amd64 users get; every benchmark rehashes one zero-filled buffer, so the 100 KB rows are cache-resident; the Intel i7-8850H tables were last edited on 2020-07-28, before the January 2023 'Improve pure Go speed up to 45%' and May 2023 AVX2/AVX-512 speedups, so they describe older code. Go version and flags are not stated for either machine.

The streaming Hasher once returned wrong hashes for payloads over 1089 bytes (issue #14, fixed September 2021), and its Write path was rewritten on 2026-09-08 ('Avoid buffered copies for chunked writes'). Reading the new block-bridging code, it keeps more than 64 unprocessed bytes whenever a block has been consumed, as XXH3's final stripe requires, but it is recent code; pin a version and keep a streaming-versus-one-shot test in your own suite.

Heavy unsafe use: []byte inputs are reinterpreted as string headers and loads use manual pointer arithmetic (open PR #32 moves to unsafe.Add). Loads are explicitly little-endian, so big-endian targets hash correctly; go-simd/xxhash reports millions of differential fuzz runs against this package, s390x included, with zero mismatches.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: No hashing library is catalogued in string-and-text (the siblings are parsers, text tools and LangArena rows). Among Go hash packages, pick it over cespare/xxhash when you need XXH3 or XXH128 values, and over go-simd/xxhash on amd64 and arm64, where go-simd's own numbers show zeebo/xxh3 faster; go-simd wins on s390x and other architectures with no SIMD path here.
verified_claims_summary: Only Go throughput is published: on a Ryzen 9 9950X (README updated 2026-07-23, Go version and flags not stated) a 64-bit hash of 100 KB takes 4.03 us with the scalar Go path, 2.10 us SSE2, 1.07 us AVX2 and 685 ns AVX-512 (149 GB/s); a 2020 i7-8850H table gives 13.0, 4.05 and 2.31 us. No C xxHash timing exists in the repository (internal/compare benchmarks cespare/xxhash, a Go XXH64), so the record shows no win over the C baseline.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-08, NEON path January 2026, five open PRs including two performance PRs) and BSD-2-Clause; easy to adopt as a Go dependency (gotosocial vendors it), but as a 'faster than C' claim it stays tier D with no measurement.
